app.name: Nexview
app.tagline: Discover new movies and shows - and request them right away.

setup.title: Welcome to Nexview
setup.intro: Start by creating your administrator account. You'll use it to manage users, approvals, and the connection to TMDB, Radarr and Sonarr.
setup.usernameHint: 3-32 characters: letters, digits, dot, hyphen, underscore.
setup.mismatch: The two passwords do not match.
setup.note: Further accounts are created later through e-mail invitations.
setup.tmdbText: TMDB provides titles, posters, descriptions and ratings. The API key is free: create an account on themoviedb.org, then go to Settings → API. Without a key, Nexview shows sample data.
setup.radarrText: Radarr handles searching and downloading movies. Find the address and API key in Radarr under Settings → General → Security. Without Radarr you cannot request movies.
setup.sonarrText: Sonarr does the same for shows. The address and API key are in Sonarr under Settings → General → Security. Without Sonarr you cannot request shows.
setup.doneText: Everything is ready. Anything you skipped can be added later under Settings. Further accounts are created through invitations under “Users”.
setup.emailHint: Used for invitations and resetting your password. It counts as confirmed right away.
setup.mailText: Nexview sends invitations and password reset links. That needs the credentials of your SMTP server.
setup.publicUrlHint: Exactly how you open Nexview in the browser. The current address is suggested.
setup.addressText: Which address do you use to open Nexview? The server cannot figure that out itself when it sits behind a reverse proxy. This address goes into every link Nexview sends later.
setup.avatarText: This is how the others recognise you in requests and approvals. Without a picture Nexview shows your initials – that is perfectly fine.
setup.verifySent: We sent a confirmation mail to {{email}}. Click the link in it and your address is verified.
setup.verifyFailed: The confirmation mail could not be sent. You can try again any time from your profile.
setup.verifyImpossible: Your e-mail address is not confirmed yet. The mail server is missing for that – add it under Settings → E-mail and start the confirmation from your profile.
setup.addressRequired: You can continue only after a successful test. Without a valid address the links in mails lead nowhere – and you would not get back in after the wizard.
setup.addressSkipHint: You can change this address later in the settings – for instance once you move to a domain of your own.
setup.mailRequired: You can continue only after a successful test. Without a mail server Nexview cannot send you the confirmation – and without that you would not get back in after the wizard.
setup.mailReady: Mail server reachable. You can continue.
setup.startText: Two ways from here. Either takes a few minutes.
setup.startFreshText: The wizard walks you through the administrator account, TMDB and the connection to Radarr and Sonarr.
setup.startRestoreText: Already have a Nexview backup? Then you keep accounts, requests and every connection instead of setting them up again.
setup.restoreText: Upload the archive you downloaded from Nexview and enter its password. Nexview first looks at what is inside — nothing is replaced until you say so.

login.title: Sign in
login.verifySent: Confirmation mail sent to {{email}}. Please also check your spam folder.
login.newAddressHint: The confirmation mail then goes to this address.

discover.title: Discover
discover.placeholder: New movies and shows from TMDB will appear here soon.
discover.placeholderHint: The TMDB connection is the next step.
discover.searchIntro: Look up a specific movie or show instead of browsing new releases.
discover.searchPrompt: Type at least two characters to search.
discover.empty: Nothing found. Try a different period or filter.
discover.demoBanner: You are seeing sample data. Once a TMDB API key is set, real new releases will appear here.

request.arrMissing: Your administrator needs to set up Radarr or Sonarr first.

state.pending_approval: This request is waiting for administrator approval.
state.failed: Something went wrong while adding this title.
state.blocked: This title is on the blocklist and cannot be requested.
state.blockedAdmin: This title is on the blocklist. It is blocked for everyone else — you can still add it.

request.seasonHint: Download just this one season. If the series is already tracked, it is not re-added - only the season is enabled.
request.moreSeasonsHint: This series is already tracked. You can request a single season - it is simply enabled in Sonarr on top.
request.targetLater: Where the title goes and in which quality is decided by the approver when they approve it.
request.futureHint: New seasons will be fetched automatically once they exist. They count as house stock, not against your quota – nobody can know in advance how large they will be.
request.allSeasonsAlready: Every season you picked is already requested or available.
request.inSubscriptionMovie: You can watch it there right now.
request.inSubscriptionSeries: Whether this season is included, the source does not say.

home.intro: What everyone wants right now - and what recently landed in your library.
home.emptyText: As soon as the first title is finished, it shows up here in full size.
home.trendingIntro: What everyone is watching this week - and you do not have yet.
home.curatedIntro: Suggestions based on the films you marked with a heart.
home.curatedEmptyText: Mark films with the heart – the more you mark, the better the suggestions fit. Nexview then builds a list from your favourites, showing only what your library is still missing.
home.curatedNothingLeft: Right now there is nothing missing that matches your favourites. Mark more films for new suggestions.

onboarding.inviteIntro: You were invited with {{email}}. Set up your account here.
onboarding.usernameHint: At least 3 characters. This is what you sign in with.
onboarding.usernameTaken: This name is already taken. Please choose another one.
onboarding.displayNameHint: How the others see you. Leave empty to use your username.
onboarding.passwordMismatch: The two passwords do not match.
onboarding.welcomeIntro: The account {{username}} was created for you. Choose your password now – nobody else knows it.
onboarding.verifiedText: Thank you – your e-mail address is now confirmed.
onboarding.expiredText: This link has expired or was already used. Please have a new one sent to you.
onboarding.forgotIntro: Enter your e-mail address. We will send you a link to choose a new password.
onboarding.readyText: Welcome to Nexview, {{username}}. You can sign in now.

mail.publicIntro: Where is Nexview reachable? This address goes into every link Nexview sends – invitations, confirmations, password resets.
mail.publicUrlHint: Exactly how you open Nexview in the browser – with https:// and no trailing slash.
mail.webhookBasisIntro: Only needed when the public address does not work for the return channel – for example inside a Docker network, or when a sign-in guard or a self-signed certificate sits in front of Nexview. Empty means the public address applies here too.
mail.webhookBasisUrlHint: Must be reachable from the machine Radarr and Sonarr run on – usually the LAN address including the port.
mail.intro: Credentials for your SMTP server. The password is stored encrypted and never shown in clear text.
mail.securityHint: When in doubt use STARTTLS on port 587. Switching suggests the usual port.
mail.usernameHint: Leave empty if the server does not require a login.
mail.passwordHint: With many providers this is a dedicated app password, not your account password.
mail.fromAddressHint: Usually has to belong to the account you log in with, otherwise the server refuses.
mail.testIntro: Nexview sends a designed test message to this address.
mail.testBlocked: Enter and save the server and sender address first.

stats.title: Statistics
stats.intro: Who requests what, what actually arrives – and how happy everyone is with it.
stats.failed: The statistics could not be loaded.
stats.unansweredHint: Written feedback nobody has replied to yet
stats.ratingSpreadHint: How often each number of stars was given.

feedback.question: How was the quality?
feedback.failed: The rating could not be saved.
feedback.outdatedHint: Radarr replaced this title with a better release. Your rating applied to the earlier file — care to rate it again?
feedback.ticketOffer: That sounds like something somebody should fix. Turn it into a ticket? Then it stays open until it has been dealt with.

myRequests.title: My requests
myRequests.intro: Every title you requested – with its current state.
myRequests.withdrawFailed: The request could not be withdrawn.
myRequests.cancelFailed: Cancelling did not work. Please try again.

adminRequests.intro: Every request from every user – approve or reject them here.
adminRequests.noPending: Nothing is waiting for your approval.
adminRequests.alsoBlockHint: Nobody can request it afterwards. It stays visible, but carries a “Blocked” badge. You can undo this any time under Settings → Blocklist.
adminRequests.storageWarnText_one: {{name}} uses {{used}} against a limit of {{limit}} – that is {{over}} over. Approving this takes up more space.
adminRequests.storageWarnText_other: {{name}} uses {{used}} against a limit of {{limit}} – that is {{over}} over. Approving these {{count}} takes up more space.
adminRequests.storageWarnHint: Putting it on hold is usually right: the request stays visible for both of you, nobody has to ask twice – and the title is still free for others.
adminRequests.inSubscriptionSeriesNote: Whether this season is included, the source does not say.

requests.cancelText: “{{title}}” will be removed from Radarr or Sonarr and no longer searched for. Your quota is freed up in return – you can request something else instead.
requests.cancelTextAdmin: “{{title}}” by {{name}} will be removed from Radarr or Sonarr and no longer searched for. {{name}}'s quota is freed up in return.
requests.cancelWarning: Any files already downloaded will be deleted as well.

logs.intro: Application log. Messages are in English because that helps when searching for errors.
logs.confirmClear: All existing entries will be deleted. New messages will still be recorded.
logs.retention: The log rotates at 5 MB (25 MB on the deep levels), keeps 3 older files and deletes everything after 14 days. The download includes the older files.
logs.levelHint: A filter always includes the higher levels: “WARNING” therefore contains the errors.
logs.modeIntro: Nexview always records — the level only decides how much. “Normal” is enough day to day; turn it up temporarily while hunting a problem.
logs.modeUntil: Switches back to “Normal” on its own at {{time}}.
logs.modeEnv: Set through the NEXVIEW_LOG_LEVEL environment variable and cannot be changed here.
logs.traceWarning: Only turn on “Everything” when someone explicitly asks for it: this level records every single database and HTTP line.

modeDesc.normal: What happened, plus warnings and errors.
modeDesc.detailed: Also the way there: every call to TMDB, Radarr, Sonarr and the media server.
modeDesc.trace: Also the raw output of third-party libraries. Very many lines.

logs.title: Log

profile.intro: Your picture, display name and password.
profile.pictureHint: PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP, up to 2 MB.
profile.name: Display name
profile.nameHint: This is how others see you in requests and approvals.
profile.mailUserImported: New account via the media server
profile.mailUserImportedHint: When someone signs in with their media server account for the first time and gets a Nexview account.
profile.mailMediaserverReconnectHint: When a media server no longer accepts your stored access and you need to sign in again.
profile.emailHint: For invitations, notifications and resetting your password.
profile.emailChanged: Address changed. Please confirm it via the link we just sent you.
profile.verificationSent: Confirmation mail is on its way.
profile.usernameHint: You sign in with this – or with your e-mail address. It cannot be changed.
profile.notificationsIntro: Everything is off by default. Only switch on what you really want to hear about by mail.
profile.notificationsBellHint: The bell in the app keeps showing everything – regardless of these switches.
profile.notificationsNeedEmail: As long as your address is unconfirmed, Nexview will not send you any mail.
profile.mailDownloadCompleteHint: As soon as a film or series you requested is in the library.
profile.mailRequestDecidedHint: When your request is approved or declined.
profile.mailRequestPending: A request is waiting for approval
profile.mailRequestPendingHint: When someone requests something you need to approve.
profile.mailFeedbackHint: When someone rates a download – and when your own feedback gets a reply.
profile.discoverDefaultsIntro: What the filter bar starts with. You can change it while browsing at any time.
profile.langRegionIntro: Applies to you alone - every user sets this themselves.
profile.themeHint: Applies to you on every device – everyone in the household can set it differently.
profile.languageHint: Applies to the interface as well as to titles and overviews. In German „Days of Thunder“ becomes „Tage des Donners“.
profile.ageRestricted: This account is age-restricted ({{age}} years). Titles rated above that are hidden from you. Only the administrator can change this.
profile.mailTicketHint: Replies to your tickets — as an administrator also every new request.
profile.mailStorageHint: When a hand-back has been decided and when a title starts taking up more space on its own. As an administrator also when someone wants to hand a title back.
profile.deleteText: Only the operator can delete your account – file the request here and it reaches them as a ticket. Your requested titles stay put for now; the operator decides what happens to them upon deletion.
profile.deleteConfirmText: The operator receives your request as a ticket and will follow up. Until then you can keep using Nexview as usual.
profile.deleteRequested: Your request has been filed – the operator will take care of it.
profile.mailChildWishHint: As soon as one of your children wishes for something and is waiting for your decision.

streaming.title: My streaming services
streaming.intro: Which subscriptions you have yourself. Request a title that already runs on one of them and Nexview says so — nothing is prevented. Leave this empty and nothing changes.
streaming.regionHint: Decides which services are offered here — and which country Nexview looks up availability for.
streaming.regionInherited: You are still on the operator's default. Check it once: it decides which services are listed here.
streaming.pickHint: Only the big subscription services. Renting, buying and free catch-up TV are deliberately left out — they cost nothing, so there is nothing to save.
streaming.noneHere: TMDB knows none of the big subscription services for this country. Check that the setting above is right.
streaming.unavailable: The list of services cannot be loaded right now.

profile.mailWatchHint: When a title you marked arrives, or a series you follow gets new episodes. Always bundled — a season pack is one mail, not eight.
profile.mailCleanupHint: At the start of each month, a mail listing what is lying around unused – biggest first. Only sent when there is something to report.
profile.signOutEverywhereText: Ends every sign-in of this account on all other devices. You stay signed in here.
profile.signOutEverywhereWarning: Useful when you suspect someone else has access. Your password stays as it is – if someone knows it, change that as well.
profile.signedOutEverywhere: All other devices have been signed out.
profile.securityIntro: Who gets into your account, and with what. Password, signed-in devices, and the tokens programs use on your behalf.

adminUsers.intro: Create accounts, set approvals and quotas.
adminUsers.noProfilesBlocked: Nothing ticked – every profile is selectable.
adminUsers.someProfilesBlocked: Ticked profiles cannot be chosen by this user.
adminUsers.noPasswordHint: This account can only get in through the media server. Disconnect it and the door is shut – until you set a password here.
adminUsers.emailHint: The welcome message with the password link goes there.
adminUsers.mailFailedTitle: Account created – but the mail did not go out
adminUsers.manualLinkHint: Pass this link on yourself. It is valid for 7 days and works only once.
adminUsers.autoApproveAdmin: always on for administrators and approvers
adminUsers.usedNow: Used in the current period: {{movies}} movies, {{series}} series
adminUsers.resetQuotaText: {{name}}'s usage in the current period is set back to zero.
adminUsers.resetQuotaHint: The existing requests are kept – only the counter starts over. At the next period change the calendar applies again.
adminUsers.quotaInvalid: “Own value” needs a whole number from 0.
adminUsers.inviteIntro: The invited person receives a mail and sets username, display name and password themselves.
adminUsers.inviteHint: The invitation is valid for 7 days. Quota and quality profiles are set on the account afterwards.
adminUsers.inviteSent: Invitation to {{email}} is on its way.
adminUsers.inviteBlocked: Invitations are not possible yet. Nexview needs the public address (Settings → Address) and a mail server (Settings → E-mail).
adminUsers.ageInvalid: Please enter an age between 0 and 21.
adminUsers.ageHint: Only titles rated for this age or below are shown. The chosen country's rating decides; where it has none, the strictest rating of any country applies. Titles without any rating are hidden – that is roughly a third of movies and over four in ten shows. This only applies within Nexview: via the media server or the file share everything remains reachable.
adminUsers.hideUnrated: Hide titles without an age rating
adminUsers.hideUnratedHint: Recommended. Switched off, titles nobody knows anything about become visible too. Switched on, “Discover” is nearly empty, because new titles usually carry no rating yet.
adminUsers.autoApproveTargetLater: the approver picks the folder – no effect
adminUsers.autoApproveTargetLaterMovies: does not apply to movies – the approver picks there
adminUsers.autoApproveTargetLaterSeries: does not apply to shows – the approver picks there
adminUsers.profilesByApprover: The approver sets the quality profile on approval – a block list would have no effect here.
adminUsers.autoApproveTargetLaterFolder: the approver picks the root folder – no effect
adminUsers.autoApproveTargetLaterProfile: the approver picks the quality profile – no effect
adminUsers.autoApproveTargetLaterBoth: the approver picks root folder and quality profile – no effect
adminUsers.dissolveItemsHint: Checked = moves to the house inventory (file stays). Unchecked is deleted via Radarr/Sonarr.
adminUsers.dissolveRunningHint: Episodes are already on disk but the order is not finished. Keeping leaves them; “keep downloading” finishes the season – completed, it falls to the house.
adminUsers.dissolveNothing: The account leaves nothing behind – no titles, no open orders.
adminUsers.dissolveSummary: {{haus}} to the house · {{del}} deleted ({{size}}) – then the account is removed for good.
adminUsers.dissolveDeleteWarning: Deleted files go through Radarr/Sonarr and land in their recycle bin, if one is set up. Without one they are gone immediately.
adminUsers.mayManageChildrenHint: Creates logins for their own children – in their profile under “Children”.
adminUsers.limitHint: Default = {{standard}}. 0 means: may not request anything.
adminUsers.resetStorageText: Everything assigned to {{name}} becomes household stock. The account starts at 0 GB afterwards.
adminUsers.resetStorageHint: No file is touched and the saved limit stays put. Pending handovers from this account count as settled afterwards.
adminUsers.storageResetDone: Storage reset – everything moved to the household.
adminUsers.dissolveOpenTitle: Approved orders with no file yet
adminUsers.dissolveOpenIntro: Nothing has downloaded yet. Ticked, the order keeps running and the title falls to the house; unticked, it is cancelled and taken out of Radarr or Sonarr.
adminUsers.dissolveOpenKeep: — keeps running, falls to the house

mediaserver.waiting: Waiting for confirmation in the Plex window …
mediaserver.codeHint: No window opened? Open the sign-in manually – your code is:
mediaserver.timeout: No confirmation arrived. Please try again.
mediaserver.profileIntro: Connect your media server accounts so you can sign in with them – your password keeps working.
mediaserver.needsPassword: You don't have a password yet. Set one before disconnecting – otherwise you won't get back in.
mediaserver.adminIntro: Connect your media server. Nexview then knows what is already in your library and who has watched what.
mediaserver.selectServer: Choose the server Nexview should use:
mediaserver.noServers: This account owns no Plex server.
mediaserver.sharedHidden_one: {{count}} server is hidden because you don't own it – libraries shared with you can't be managed.
mediaserver.sharedHidden_other: {{count}} servers are hidden because you don't own them – libraries shared with you can't be managed.
mediaserver.autoImportHint: Anyone with access to your library gets an account on first sign-in. When off, only people you already invited can connect.
mediaserver.libraryIntro: Nexview reads what sits in your media server libraries — and spots titles that never came through Radarr/Sonarr. They show up as "In the library" and cannot be requested twice. Runs hourly in the background.
mediaserver.disconnectLinked_one: {{count}} account is linked to this server.
mediaserver.disconnectLinked_other: {{count}} accounts are linked to this server.
mediaserver.disconnectAllSafe: They all have a way in of their own – nobody gets locked out.
mediaserver.disconnectKeeps: The links stay saved. Connect the same server again later and everything is as it was.
mediaserver.disconnectLocksOut_one: {{count}} account has no password of its own and could not get back in:
mediaserver.disconnectLocksOut_other: {{count}} accounts have no password of their own and could not get back in:
mediaserver.disconnectFix: Give those accounts a password first – under Settings ▸ Users.
mediaserver.tileSoonHint: Coming in one of the next versions.
mediaserver.newAccountsUnlimited: New accounts get no request limit. To give one person a limit, set it on the invitation or afterwards under Settings ▸ Users.
mediaserver.newAccountsStorage: New accounts get the house allowance of {{gb}} GB. Change it under Settings ▸ Storage quotas.
mediaserver.newAccountsStorageUnlimited: New accounts get the house allowance — which is currently unlimited. Change it under Settings ▸ Storage quotas.
mediaserver.passwordIntro: {{name}} has no intermediary the way Plex does. The address, username and password go straight to the server – Nexview keeps only the token that comes back.
mediaserver.serverAddressHint: The address Nexview reaches the server at – not necessarily the one you use in your browser.
mediaserver.adminUserHint: An account with administrator rights. Only such an account lets Nexview read the server's users.
mediaserver.adminPasswordHint: Not stored. It is used once, to obtain a token.
mediaserver.blocksIntroFor: These {{name}} accounts no longer get a new Nexview account. Entries appear when a user is deleted.
mediaserver.linkSoon: Linking arrives in one of the next versions.
mediaserver.noLoginYet: Anyone who has already linked their {{name}} account can sign in with it. New accounts are not created this way: {{name}} does not give an email address for an account, and without one Nexview could not tell whether someone already has an account. Those who do link {{name}} in their profile under "Security".
mediaserver.noNewAccountHint: Already have a Nexview account? Sign in with it and link {{name}} in your profile – {{name}} alone does not create an account.
mediaserver.serverGone: The server is not connected right now – the link stays until an administrator connects it again.
mediaserver.selectServerHint: On connecting, Nexview reads the whole library right away – with large collections that can take a minute.
mediaserver.connectSlow: This can take a few minutes — Nexview is reading the server's library. Please do not reload the page.

settings.title: Settings
settings.intro: These credentials are stored encrypted in the database and never leave the server.
settings.tmdbHint: Create a free API key at themoviedb.org under Account → Settings → API.
settings.defaultProfileMissing: Enter and save the API key first, then the profiles can be loaded.
settings.defaultProfileHint: Preselected for everyone. If it is blocked for someone, their first allowed profile is used instead.
settings.keySetHint: A key is stored. Leave empty to keep it.
settings.webhookVersionHint: Radarr or Sonarr tells Nexview right away instead of waiting for the 2-minute cycle. Works with Radarr 5 and Sonarr 4 or newer; Nexview checks older instances itself and names what is missing. Nexview creates and maintains the entry over there – unticking removes it without leftovers.
settings.webhookNeverProven: No call has ever arrived – the proof is still missing.

webhookReason.no_address: There is no address Radarr/Sonarr could reach Nexview at – set one under “Address”.
webhookReason.too_old: This instance is too old for the return channel.
webhookReason.proof_failed: The test call never arrived. Can the instance reach the address? Behind a reverse proxy: sign-in guard, certificate or router – the “address as seen by Radarr/Sonarr” bypasses all of that.
webhookReason.unreachable: The instance could not be reached.
webhookReason.create_failed: The entry could not be written.

settings.arrHint: Find the API key in Radarr/Sonarr under Settings → General → Security.
settings.updateCheckHint: Nexview asks GitHub at most once a day whether a newer version exists. No data from Nexview is transmitted.
settings.languageHint: Applies to newly invited accounts and to mail sent to people without an account. Anyone signed in can switch language at the top right - titles and descriptions follow automatically.
settings.regionHint: Default for everyone who has not set their own in their profile.
settings.rootFolderChoice: Let users pick the root folder
settings.rootFolderChoiceHint: When off, users no longer see a folder field when requesting - the default folder set below applies to everyone. Administrators keep the free choice.
settings.defaultRootHint: Everything goes there while the choice is switched off.
settings.rootFolderSectionHint: Applies to the standard and the 4K instance alike – who may pick is a house rule, not a property of the instance.
settings.instanceStandardHint: The regular instance – everything not explicitly requested in 4K ends up here.
settings.targetSectionHint: Applies to the standard and the 4K instance alike – who may pick is a house rule, not a property of the instance.
settings.profileModeHint_user: A list of profiles appears when requesting. Individual ones can be blocked per user.
settings.profileModeHint_fixed: Users see no profile field; the one set below applies to everyone. Administrators still pick freely.
settings.profileModeHint_approver: The request arrives without a profile and waits for approval; it is picked there.
settings.approverEndsAutoApprove: Note: as soon as the profile or the root folder is left to the approver, no request for this service can go through automatically – it would be incomplete. Users’ auto-approval has no effect for this service; the stored setting is kept and applies again once you switch back. Anyone who may approve still picks when requesting.
settings.rootFolderModeHint_user: A list of the folders from Radarr or Sonarr appears when requesting.
settings.rootFolderModeHint_fixed: Users see no folder field; the folder set below applies to everyone. Administrators still pick freely.
settings.rootFolderModeHint_approver: For libraries split across several folders — by genre, for example. Requests arrive without a folder or profile and always wait for approval; both are picked there. Anyone who may approve still picks when requesting.
settings.targetPairCoupled: Root folder and quality profile belong together: once the approver picks one of them, the request waits for them anyway – so they set the other one too. That is why it moved along.
settings.secretsUnreadable: Stored credentials (API keys, media server access) can no longer be read with the current secret key. Most common cause: NEXVIEW_SECRET_KEY was changed, or data/secret.key was lost when the container was recreated (file not inside the mounted volume). Re-enter the affected credentials or reconnect the media server once – and make sure the key is kept permanently, or this will happen again on the next update.

errors.generic: Something went wrong. Please try again.
errors.network: The backend is unreachable. Is the server running?
errors.sessionExpired: Your session has expired. Please sign in again.
errors.internal: The server ran into an error. Number for troubleshooting: {{id}}

errors.tooManyAttemptsSeconds_other: Too many failed attempts. Please try again in {{count}} seconds.
errors.tooManyAttemptsMinutes_one: Too many failed attempts. Please try again in a minute — it opens again by itself.
errors.tooManyAttemptsMinutes_other: Too many failed attempts. Please try again in {{count}} minutes — it opens again by itself.

byCode.account_disabled_ask_admin: This account is switched off. Please ask your administrator.
byCode.account_exists_sign_in: There is already an account for that address. Just sign in.
byCode.apikey_needs_name: Give the key a name so you recognise it later.
byCode.apikey_not_for_children: Child accounts do not get access keys.
byCode.apikey_too_many: More than 20 keys per account is not supported.
byCode.approvers_only: Only administrators and approvers can do that.
byCode.arr_instance_missing: This instance is not set up.
byCode.arr_key_rejected: {{service}} did not accept the API key.
byCode.arr_media_management_missing: The instance is not returning its media management settings.
byCode.arr_nothing_to_delete: There are no files to delete.
byCode.arr_path_unknown: {{service}} answers, but does not know this address. Does the URL really point to {{service}}?
byCode.arr_unexpected_answer: The answer from {{service}} was unexpected. Does the address really point to {{service}}?
byCode.arr_unreachable: {{service}} cannot be reached at {{url}}. Are the address and port correct?
byCode.auth_mode_invalid: The sign-in has to be 'none', 'basic' or 'token'.
byCode.backup_failed: The backup could not be created.
byCode.bad_credentials: That username or password is wrong.
byCode.blocklist_admins_only: Only an administrator can put a title on the block list.
byCode.cannot_delete_self: You cannot delete your own account.
byCode.cannot_demote_self: You cannot take your own administrator rights away.
byCode.category_unknown_here: There is no such category here.
byCode.category_unknown_there: There is no such category there.
byCode.children_only: This view is only for children's accounts.
byCode.connection_incomplete: Some connection details are still missing.
byCode.current_password_wrong: That is not your current password.
byCode.date_range_reversed: The start date is after the end date.
byCode.demo_mode_invalid: The demo mode has to be 'auto', 'on' or 'off'.

about.title: About Nexview
about.tagline: Discover new releases, request them, and let Radarr and Sonarr download them automatically.
about.updateHint: To update, run »docker compose pull« on the server, then »docker compose up -d«. Your database is kept; Nexview backs it up automatically before changing it.
about.creditsIntro: Nexview stands on other people's shoulders. These services and components make it possible.
about.tmdbNotice: All information about films, series, cast and images comes from TMDB. Nexview uses the TMDB API but is not endorsed or certified by TMDB.
about.arrNotice: They do the actual downloading. Nexview only passes requests along.
about.plexNotice: Sign-in, library sync and "already seen" – provided a media server is connected. Nexview is neither supported by nor affiliated with Plex or Jellyfin.
about.justwatchNotice: Source of the streaming availability on title pages (“Where to stream”). TMDB passes this data through from JustWatch.
about.youtubeNotice: Trailers play from there. TMDB only supplies the reference.
about.ratingsNotice: Their scores appear on films. Nexview does not fetch them directly; it takes them from Radarr, which supplies them with every movie. The trademarks belong to their respective owners.
about.seerrNotice: Seerr, which grew out of Overseerr and Jellyseerr, showed what a request interface for Radarr and Sonarr can look like – from the second 4K instance to matching against the media server. Nexview is an independent implementation and shares no source code, but owes Seerr many of its ideas.
about.notifyNotice: Deliver the system notifications, where set up. Nexview is not affiliated with any of these services.

telegram.title: Setting up Telegram
telegram.intro: Telegram takes more preparation than the other services: an account, a bot and a chat ID. All of it happens inside Telegram, not here. On a computer it takes about five minutes.

account.title: Create a Telegram account
account.body: Nothing works without one. Telegram requires a phone number to sign up and sends the confirmation code by SMS. Either the Windows program or the browser version will do. If you already use Telegram on your phone, skip this step.

botfather.title: Open BotFather
botfather.body: Bots are created by a bot: @BotFather is the official way. Open the chat and send /start.

newbot.title: Create the bot
newbot.body: Send /newbot. BotFather first asks for a display name – freely chosen, for example “Nexview”. Then for a username; it must be unique and end in “bot”, for example “nexview_home_bot”.

token.title: Copy the token
token.body: BotFather replies with a token in the form 123456789:AAG… That is the key to your bot – whoever holds it can post in its name. Treat it like a password.

instance.title: Back in Nexview: enter the bot
instance.body: From here on you work in the left column again. Under “Label”, enter a name of your choosing – it only appears on the tile later and has nothing to do with Telegram, for example “Home”. Below that, paste the token from step 4 into “Bot token”.

startchat.title: Message the bot once
startchat.body: After saving, Nexview shows you this step itself, with a link and a button to tick it off. The reason behind it: a bot may never message anyone first. Only once you have sent it /start may it write to you – no answer comes back, there is no program behind the bot.

group.title: Direct chat or group?
group.body: If the messages are only for you, skip this – your own chat with the bot is enough. If several people should read along, create a group in Telegram, add your bot as a member and post something there. In the next step both appear to choose from: your name for the direct chat, the group's name for the group.

finish.title: Add the chat and confirm it
finish.body: Press “Add chat” and “Fetch chats from the bot” – clicking an entry takes over both number and label. Then “Send test message”: a message with a four-digit code arrives in Telegram. Enter it and press “Check”. Only then do the tick boxes appear with which you choose what this chat should report – and then save.

checktoken.title: Press “Check token”, then save
checktoken.body: Nexview asks Telegram whether the token is valid. If it is, the “Bot username” field fills itself and a link to your bot appears below it. Now press “Save” on the right – there is no way past this, because only afterwards are there any chats to add.

0.22.0.lead: This release is about a question most people ask too late: **what happens when something breaks?** Nexview can now make backups you can download and take with you — and put them back, even on a fresh installation. On top of that comes an interface with a promise, so something other than a browser can finally talk to Nexview.

sections.title: Backups you can take with you
sections.body:
Nexview has always put a copy aside before every database change — but that copy sat in the same directory as the database. Lose the volume and it goes too.

Now you can make one on demand, give it a note, and **download it**. What you get is an **encrypted ZIP** holding the database, the profile pictures and the key file `secret.key`. The key has to come along: your credentials for Radarr, Sonarr, TMDB and the mail server are encrypted with it, and without it they cannot be read again. That is why the archive needs a password — and why it is a plain AES ZIP rather than a format of our own. You can open it with 7-Zip, without Nexview.

**Caches are stripped out.** Nine tenths of the database is stored TMDB answers and the library comparison — both of which Nexview fetches again by itself. That is why a backup is a few megabytes rather than a few hundred.

On a schedule too: daily, weekly or monthly, weekly by default. Automatic backups are marked as such, and you set how many are kept.

sections.title: Restore — including on a fresh installation
sections.where: In the setup wizard, first question
sections.body:
An empty installation now asks first: **start fresh, or restore from a backup?** Anyone moving house or coming back from an outage no longer has to walk the whole wizard and then rebuild everything by hand.

**It checks first whether the backup even fits.** Nexview can only migrate its database forward, never back — so a backup from a *newer* version is refused rather than restored. That is not paternalism: restoring it would break the installation, and quietly.

Before restoring, Nexview saves a copy of the current state. And afterwards **every sign-in everywhere is ended** — including your own. That is deliberate: the accounts in the backup may not be the ones from a minute ago.

sections.title: API tokens
sections.body:
For scripts, dashboards and anything that talks to Nexview without a browser. You create one, name it, and the plain text appears **exactly once** — afterwards only a checksum remains, and not even an administrator can look it up.

**A token has exactly the rights of its account.** No more. Role, quota, approval and blocklist apply to it just as they apply to you. This is deliberately unlike Seerr, where a single global key is tied to the owner account and therefore gets everything auto-approved. If you want a service account with few rights, create a *user* with those rights and give it a token.

One switch on top: **may only read** — right for dashboards and monitoring. Tokens can expire, the list shows when each was last used, and revoking one takes effect immediately. Child accounts get none.

Administrators see under *Settings → System → API tokens* who holds which and whether they are still in use. **Look, do not revoke** — only the owner can do that.

sections.title: A promise for developers: /api/v1
sections.body:
Nexview has around 190 addresses, and nearly all of them are internal: the interface talks to the backend, both change together, and a field gets a different name tomorrow when the new one fits better. For anyone wiring something up from outside, that is unusable.

So **thirteen** addresses live under `/api/v1` — with a promise: as long as `v1` is in the address, nothing disappears from those answers. If something has to break, `/api/v2` appears **beside** it and v1 keeps running.

They cover what you actually do with such an interface: find something, request it, check what became of it, and a few numbers for a dashboard. **Everything else stays reachable** — just without the promise. Administration is deliberately excluded: promising it would mean freezing the configuration model.

sections.title: Sign out everywhere
sections.body:
Ends every sign-in of this account on every device — including the one you are sitting at.

This closed a real hole: until now, signing out only worked in your own browser. If you had left your account open on someone else’s machine, there was nothing you could do about it; even a new password only helped against future sign-ins, not running ones.

sections.title: Dissolving an account without collateral damage
sections.body:
When an account was deleted, its already **approved** requests were cancelled along with it. In a household that is almost always wrong: the film has long since arrived, someone else watches it too, and the order vanished with the account.

Now approved requests move into the **house collection** — they stay, just without an owner. Only what is still open gets cancelled. The preview before deleting says what will happen, instead of showing it afterwards.

sections.title: Tidied up
sections.body:
The settings bar had grown to ten entries and wrapped on narrow screens. *Address*, *Mail*, *Log* and *Backups* are pulled together under **System**, and every tab carries an icon.

Your **profile** got a sub-menu: *Profile* (picture, name, email, light or dark), *Security* (password, signed-in devices, API tokens) and *Language*. Before, six blocks sat stacked on one page, and the most useful thing was furthest down.

The real cause lay deeper: there were **three** different implementations of a sub-navigation row, and the component that draws a highlighted settings block existed only inside a single page. Both now live in one place, so the pages cannot drift apart again.

small: The interface documentation at `/docs` was a **blank white page** — in every installation, since 0.21.0. It loads Swagger UI, which FastAPI fetched from a foreign server; but the content rules we added in that same release only allow scripts from Nexview itself. The browser refused both stylesheet and script and rendered nothing. It went unnoticed because the rules were tested against the *application*, and the application kept working. Swagger UI now ships inside the image and is served by Nexview: the rules stay as strict as they were, and the documentation works on a machine with no internet at all. `/redoc` was blank for the same reason and served the web interface instead — it now leads to `/docs`.

The thirteen promised endpoints describe themselves in **English**. Every explanation in the source is German, because that is the language this is written in — and FastAPI put those same explanations on the public page. The remaining 151 are still German; none of them is promised to anyone.

A brand-new installation wrote a backup of the **empty** database. On the very first start the check reports that everything is missing, and Nexview dutifully made a copy that protected nothing while using up a slot.

0.21.0.lead: This release tidies up, in the literal sense. Nexview can now show you what has been lying around for a long time with nobody watching it: how much room it takes, when it was last watched, and who it is attributed to. Deleting is not a button that takes effect at once but a suggestion with fourteen days to think it over. And staying signed in now lives somewhere no script can reach.

sections.title: What is lying around unused
sections.where: Statistics → its own entry at the top
sections.body:
A list of the titles nobody has watched in a long time — biggest first. With how much room each one takes, when it last ran, **who watched it**, and who it is attributed to. Filter by movies or series, search by title, and set the period from a few months up to several years.

**Two clocks count, not one.** A title only appears if nobody watched it within the chosen period *and* it has been here at least that long. Without the second clock the list would effectively be sorted by size, and yesterday’s 60 GB file would sit right at the top of it, before anyone had the chance to watch it.

What Nexview does *not* know, it says: items whose arrival date is still missing are counted and named, instead of quietly disappearing.

sections.title: Deleting has a grace period now
sections.body:
Marking something does not delete it. It sets a date **fourteen days** out; until then the title stays, visibly marked, and one click takes the mark away again.

**Anyone who watches it in the meantime cancels the deletion on their own** — without ever learning there was one. That is the real point of the grace period: it catches exactly the case where a list looks right and is wrong anyway.

sections.title: A mail once a month
sections.body:
Nexview can send you monthly what is lying around: thirty lines at most, biggest first, with a link straight into the list.

**Off by default.** And without a mail server and a public address nothing goes out at all — a mail with a button that leads nowhere would be worse than no mail.

sections.title: Your own titles, and how to hand them back
sections.body:
The same list, but only for what is attributed to you — and from there you can hand something back.

That the list stays empty for many people at first is the normal case, not a fault: everything that was already here before Nexview counts as **house inventory** and belongs to nobody. Nexview now says so, instead of showing an empty page.

sections.title: Requests that were put aside come back
sections.body: A deferred request stayed deferred. It now reappears under open approvals as soon as it fits again.

sections.title: Staying signed in is out of reach now
sections.where: Nowhere to be seen — which is exactly the point
sections.body:
The proof that you are signed in used to sit in the browser’s storage, where **any script on the page could read it**. It now lives in a cookie that JavaScript never gets to see at all, that only travels to the sign-in addresses, and that is not sent along from other sites.

**Changing your password now really does end every other session.** The description had said so for a long time without it being true.

Alongside it, a rule for the browser: it runs only code that came from Nexview itself, and loads images only from the handful of addresses the covers come from. Should anything ever get a foreign script onto the page, the browser turns it away before it runs.

⚠️ What this does **not** cover: signing out only takes the cookie out of *this* browser. Anyone who made a copy beforehand keeps getting in until it expires. That was no different before — but it deserves saying out loud instead of sitting in a description. Today the only way to really end someone else’s session is to change your password.

small: Ratings on a movie page had been returning an error since 0.19.0 — **every** call, in 0.19.0 and in 0.20.0. A rewrite had left one caller behind and nobody noticed. A test now walks the whole codebase for calls into functions that no longer exist.
Two of the mail switches in the profile were saved nowhere. The list of switches is now derived from the data model itself — the next one cannot be forgotten the same way.
Storage was counted twice whenever Radarr and the media server report the same file under different quality levels. On a grown library that adds up to hundreds of gigabytes that were never there.
Bold text showed its asterisks in several places — most visibly in this very window.
A series tile now says which seasons are here, instead of looking the same whether one arrived or all of them.

0.20.0.lead: There is barely anything to look at in this release — and it is still one of the most important so far. Signing in gets a brake: until now a machine could try passwords as fast as the line allowed. And the error messages finally speak the language you picked.

sections.title: Signing in now has a brake
sections.where: Nowhere to be seen — which is exactly the point
sections.body:
Until now there was no rate limit and no lock at all. Anyone who knew the address of your installation could try passwords as fast as the line allowed.

After three wrong attempts the wait grows: one second, two, four. After ten the door stays shut for fifteen minutes. **It opens again by itself** — a lock that needs an administrator to open it ends up locking out the administrator. And hammering on a closed door extends nothing: otherwise a stranger could keep someone locked out for good simply by not stopping.

**There are three doors, not one.** Besides signing in to Nexview there is signing in with your *media server* password — and that one is the worse of the two: Nexview hands the password to Plex, Jellyfin or Emby, and it needs no Nexview account at all. Without a brake, Nexview was a comfortable way to guess passwords against your own media server, with somebody else's return address on it. The links sent by mail are covered too.

Anyone who knows their password notices none of this. A wrong password counts; a switched-off account or an unconfirmed address does not — those are people waiting for something else.

sections.title: When a reverse proxy sits in front
sections.body:
Attempts are always counted **per account**, and that needs no setting.

Counting per address as well only works if Nexview knows the real one, and it cannot tell on its own. Behind a reverse proxy every request looks like it comes from the same address — the proxy's. If Nexview simply assumed otherwise, the first typo would lock out the whole household, you included.

So it does not guess, it asks: `direct` if Nexview is reachable directly, `proxy` for one in front, `proxy:2` for two (say Cloudflare and then your own). Your proxy has to pass `X-Forwarded-For` — Nginx Proxy Manager, Caddy and Traefik do that on their own.

⚠️ **Leave it empty if unsure.** That is always safe, and the per-account lock still works.

sections.title: Error messages come in your language
sections.body:
The interface has been bilingual from the first day. The messages from the server never were: switch to English, mistype your password, and up came „Benutzername oder Passwort ist falsch.“ Hardly anyone noticed, because you have to make a mistake to see one.

All 76 of them speak both languages now. The server does not translate — it **names**. It cannot know which language you picked: that choice lives in your browser, and on the sign-in page there is not even an account to hang a language on. A server translating there would have to guess, and would guess wrong for exactly the person who switched on purpose.

Two kinds stay as they are: what Plex, Jellyfin or Emby report back arrives in *their* language. Translating that would mean inventing it.

sections.title: The port inside the container can be moved
sections.body:
Nexview listened on a fixed 8000. In the normal case that never shows, because the port mapping hides it. But with `network_mode: host` there is no mapping — there the port inside the container *is* the port on your server, and nothing helped against a collision.

`NEXVIEW_PORT` moves it. Left empty, everything stays as it was.

Reported by the TrueNAS catalogue reviewer while Nexview was being taken in. It applies to Unraid and plain Docker just the same.

small: Error replies were losing their headers — everywhere a built frontend sits next to the backend, which is to say in every container. Nothing looked wrong: the status was right, the text was right, only half the reply was missing.

0.19.0.lead: This release brings Emby as a third media server, opens up rating to everyone — and merges the quotas: item count and storage space now apply together instead of either-or. Along with it, several places where Nexview finally says what it long knew: why a request is taking time, what is already in your own subscription, and when a title you were waiting for has arrived.

sections.title: Emby, as a third media server
sections.body:
Connecting, signing in, syncing the library, watched state per person — all as before, just with one more server. Running them side by side is unchanged: connect Plex, Jellyfin and Emby at the same time if you like, and the watched state is merged across all three.

One limit is worth knowing: Emby accounts have no e-mail address either. Signing in through Emby therefore does not create an account — you link it from your profile. Without an address there is nothing for Nexview to recognise someone by, and an invitation would quietly end up as a second account with no password.

The PIN Emby optionally keeps per account is not in the way: it belongs to the display settings, not to permissions — a profile PIN for switching on a shared device, the kind you know from Netflix.

sections.title: Anyone can rate, not just the requester
sections.where: On every title page for a title you already have
sections.body:
Quality feedback used to hang on the request. Everything else followed from that: only whoever ordered saw the stars — and anyone who watched the same film two weeks later and noticed the audio track was missing had no way to say so.

This is not about taste, that is what the heart is for, but about the **file** — and anyone who has watched it can judge that equally well. Ratings therefore hang on the title now. In “My requests” the stars remain as a shortcut, because the moment right after “already downloaded” is when people rate.

Series are judged per season: the files sit per season, the quality differs per season. Existing ratings move across on first start.

sections.title: “Tell me when it arrives” — waiting without requesting
sections.where: On the title page, when someone else has already requested it
sections.body:
Until now a title that had already been requested could not be requested again — and after that the second person never heard about it again. They were not even told when it arrived, which was exactly their question.

For a **film** the button sits where “searching” otherwise stands, so exactly when there is something to wait for. You are told once, then the reminder is done. For a **series** it sits permanently next to the request button and reports every new episode — that is usually what you are waiting for.

Reports are always bundled: a season pack of eight episodes is *one* message, and consecutive numbers are collapsed (“S2: 1–3, 7”). Eight messages in the same minute would be the fastest way to make someone turn notifications off.

sections.title: What is already in your subscription
sections.where: Profile → Streaming services, shown when requesting
sections.body:
Anyone who lists their streaming services gets the one sentence that can change the decision: “This is on your Netflix.” A **hint**, not a block — nothing is prevented.

For series a deliberately different sentence appears: the source says “on Netflix” about the *series*, not about the fourth season that is missing there — and that is exactly the case in which someone requests it.

The same check appears where decisions are made: in the approval list, and for parents deciding on a child's wish. It is measured against the **requester's** subscriptions, not the approver's — they may not have Netflix, but the question is whether the requester could do without the download.

sections.title: The history of a request
sections.body:
“Why is this taking so long?” is the most common question, and Nexview always knew the full answer — requested when, approved by whom, searching since when, last checked when. All that was visible was a single status word.

A button now opens a timeline: completed steps green with a tick, the running one yellow, upcoming ones grey. A path that was cut short ends where it ends — below a rejection there is no grey “done” step that would be a promise nobody keeps.

Two pieces of information reach the requester for the first time: who approved it (or that it was automatic) and when the title was last checked on.

sections.title: One tab instead of a mode switch
sections.body:
Until now a switch decided whether the number of requests counted or the space used — never both. It is gone. Instead there are three defaults: movies, series, storage. They apply to anyone without a value of their own.

A request goes through when both limits still have room. When someone is stopped, the message says which of the two it was — a full item count is cured by waiting, full storage only by clearing up. Without that you would have to guess.

The period for the item count (day, week, month) now applies house-wide. It used to sit on every account; three accounts with three different periods no longer explain to anyone what “3 movies” actually means.

sections.title: Three states instead of an empty field
sections.body:
Every account now shows all three limits side by side, each with the same choice: **default** (the value from the quota settings, with the actual number next to it), **unlimited**, or a **value of your own**. A 0 means “may not request anything”.

Before, “unlimited” was an empty field. Anyone who had typed a number once could not see how to get back.

⚠️ One meaning has flipped: for storage, **0** used to mean “unlimited for this account”. Now it means the opposite. Stored zeroes move to “unlimited” automatically on first start — otherwise an account would have been silently locked overnight.

sections.title: Seeing and handing over storage is available everywhere
sections.body:
The storage tab, the household stock and the hand-over button hung on the old master switch — anyone limiting by item count never saw them. Measuring always happens, limiting only on request, so the whole chain is now open to everyone: hand over, the operator decides, the title goes to the household, stays, or is deleted.

For operators that means a handover may now land on your desk that never used to arrive.

⚠️ If you have been limiting by item count, every account starts at zero once — everything assigned becomes household stock. The GB limits were inert in that mode while the assignment kept running in the background. Without this step people would be locked out right after the update because of a number that had been lying around for months. No file is touched.

sections.title: Titles Radarr and Sonarr no longer know
sections.body:
Removing a title from Radarr while keeping the file creates something Nexview keeps counting — the media server still reports it — but can no longer remove: deletion happens exclusively through Radarr and Sonarr. The requester was left carrying a load they could not shed.

Such rows now carry a marker with an explanation. Until now only the operator noticed, and only at the moment they tried to delete the title.

sections.title: Resetting is a button, not a side effect
sections.body:
Switching modes used to silently reset every account to zero. That operation is still there, but now as its own button with a confirmation: “Move everything to the household” in the quota settings, “Reset storage” on every individual account.

Both state the numbers first. No file is touched, saved limits stay put — and pending handovers count as settled afterwards.

The per-account button is also the way out of the case above: if someone is stuck with a title Radarr no longer manages, this clears it.

small: The region picker now knows 139 countries instead of eight — anyone in the Netherlands, Poland or Canada simply could not state their country before.
A yellow bar is a reminder to set your own region. For “this is on your Netflix” the operator's inherited default is a false claim — the Netflix Switzerland catalogue is not the German one.
Ratings are marked as outdated when Radarr upgrades the file afterwards. They stay put but no longer count — and the person affected may rate again.
The feedback view now shows every rating, not just those with a request behind them.
One or two stars can be turned into a ticket — a problem otherwise disappears into an average.
Statistics show movies, series and storage side by side instead of either-or.
The approval dialog warns when the requester is already over their storage limit — that warning used to exist only in GB mode.

0.18.0.lead: Nexview now talks to Jellyfin as well — alongside Plex, not instead of it. Both servers may be connected at the same time, and each person can link an account on each. Around that sits a set of changes that stop anyone being locked out by accident, and a log you can actually find faults with.

sections.title: Jellyfin alongside Plex
sections.body:
Both servers may be connected at once, and the watched state is merged across them: a title stays marked as seen while any connected server still reports it — so adding a second server no longer wipes the ticks the first one gave you.

Where the two disagree, Nexview now says which server reports what, instead of quietly picking one.

sections.title: The sign-in page shows the ways that exist
sections.body:
Instead of a fixed “Sign in with Plex” it now says “Sign in with” and offers one logo per connected server. An installation running only Jellyfin used to get a Plex button that failed on click — the flow behind it is built around plex.tv, which Jellyfin has no equivalent for.

One limit is worth knowing: signing in with Jellyfin will not create an account. Jellyfin gives no email address for an account, and the address is the only thing that lets Nexview recognise somebody who already has one. Without it, an invited person would quietly end up with a second account — no password, no way back in. Those who have an account link Jellyfin from their profile instead; the sign-in form says so before anyone falls into it.

sections.title: Media server accounts have their own place
sections.body: They used to sit at the very bottom of “Security”, below the password form. Nobody looking to connect Plex would think to search there.

sections.title: Disconnecting no longer locks people out by accident
sections.where: Settings → Media servers and Settings → Users
sections.body:
Disconnecting the media server used to happen on a single click, without a word. For accounts that only ever came in through that server — with no password of their own — this closed their only door.

A confirmation now counts them by name beforehand, and the server refuses outright unless the administrator explicitly overrides it. The same check already guarded people disconnecting themselves; it was missing one level up. The dialog also appears when nobody is at risk and says so: a warning that only ever shows up in an emergency is not read the first time it matters.

The user list also shows who is linked and who has no password. Both facts were already known to the app and shown nowhere.

sections.title: The log finally finds faults
sections.body:
Crashes land in the file at last. Before, uvicorn wrote them somewhere Nexview's own log never reached: you downloaded the log, and precisely the crash was missing from it.

Every request gets a short number that appears in every line it produces — and in the error message. The user passes on six characters, the administrator types them into the search and sees the complete course of that one click, instead of guessing at timestamps.

Four levels, switchable while running: Quiet, Normal, Detailed and Everything. The two deep levels switch themselves back off after 30 minutes, 2 hours or 8 hours — a forgotten diagnostic level would otherwise overwrite the very lines it was turned on to capture.

sections.title: Nexview is now under the AGPL
sections.body:
The source stays public and free, and running Nexview unchanged asks nothing of you. What changes concerns those who build on it: anyone who modifies Nexview and lets others use their version — including as a hosted service, where no file ever changes hands — has to make their changed source available too.

Versions up to and including 0.17.0 stay under the MIT licence. That permission was given for good and is not being taken back.

small: A second media server displaced the first: every account held exactly one media server identity, in a handful of columns. Connecting Jellyfin while linked to Plex overwrote that link without a word — name, address and the personal token. Identities now live in a table of their own, one row per provider.

Each server keeps its own access. Jellyfin issues tokens per device, and Nexview announced itself under a single device name for everything: signing in personally therefore revoked the administrator's server connection, and two people signing in revoked each other.

The library count on a server's page was not that server's: it counted across all connected servers and showed the same number on every page. The page now shows only when it last synced, and the button syncs only the server whose page it is.

One unreadable notification silenced the whole bell: the list said “nothing new” while the counter beside it kept claiming unread messages. Measured in a real database, four such rows had been hiding a genuine unread piece of feedback for a week.

The comment above passwordless accounts was lying: it claimed such an account could set a password later in its profile. It cannot — that route demands the current password, which the account never had. The two routes that do work are written down there now.
The level filter in the log hid errors: choosing “WARNING” compared for equality and therefore left out the ERROR lines, exactly the ones being looked for. A level now means “this level and above”.
The watchlist hint pointed at the wrong tab — it sent people to “Security” to link their account, which is where media server accounts lived until this release.
Downloading the log now includes the rotated files. During a hunt the interesting section has often already rolled over into the previous file.

0.17.0.lead: Nexview can browse now. Until today, Discover only showed a rolling window of at most a year — everything older was reachable by search alone. The new area opens the whole catalogue, and beside it sits a guide that asks you a few questions and then suggests something for tonight.

sections.title: What to watch?
sections.body:
The guide asks: who is watching, what are you in the mood for, does it have to play tonight, how much time is there, something new or something familiar. Six questions at most — and the tree adapts: choosing “only what's already here” drops the hidden-gem question, because in your own library it has no meaning. It ends in twelve suggestions, and “Roll again” gives you a different set.

“With children” sets a real age rating (FSK 6 at most), not guessed genres. Nothing is taken away for it: a scare stays selectable and then returns “The House with a Clock in Its Walls” and “The Witches” instead of grown-up horror.

sections.title: Browse
sections.body:
Shelves instead of a time window: “Hidden gems” (well rated, barely known), “Timeless classics”, “Under 90 minutes”, “Newly released”, plus five decades and every genre. Every shelf works on an empty library and without any personal data.

At the top sits the question that comes first on movie night: “Does it have to play tonight?” Unlike before, this is sieved on the server — with a full library the rows stay full instead of shrinking to two tiles.

sections.title: Filter yourself
sections.body:
Six questions instead of thirteen controls: how much time, what you are after (genres can be included and excluded), which era (real decades), how well known, already here or not, and the order.

The runtime ceiling is genuinely new — “we only have ninety minutes” could not be expressed at all before. And what you set lives in the address: you can send a result to someone or bookmark it.

sections.title: Your own shelves
sections.body:
“Not seen in a while” takes what is at least six months back — if there is nothing like that, the shelf disappears instead of suggesting something that does not fit. “Because you like X” gives every favourite its own row, so it stays clear why something is suggested.

At most three of them: one slot always belongs to your newest favourite, the others change daily. With a hundred favourites you see all of them over time instead of the same three.

sections.title: The menu is shorter
sections.body: “Discover movies” and “Discover series” have left the menu. Browse answers every one of their questions better — except one, “what came out recently?”, and that is now the “Newly released” shelf. The addresses still work, so old bookmarks do not break.

sections.title: Calendar tidied up
sections.body:
Instead of “Everything / already requested” it now says “Films & episodes / Films only / Episodes only” — your own titles already sit at the top of each day, so the useful split is between film and episode.

And the strictness filter no longer asks either for big studios or for known titles, but for both: measured against a real week, neither finds what the other finds — the studio list catches brand-new series with no votes, the vote floor catches good titles without a big distributor.

small: “Highest rated” returned noise instead of good films: TMDB has no weighted ranking and the floor was five votes, so a film with twenty votes and a 9.4 average outranked “The Godfather”. It is 300 now. This also repairs the sort on the old Discover page.
A runtime limit was not kept. TMDB's own filter is unreliable — asking for at most 95 minutes returned a 97- and a 99-minute film. The runtime is checked again on the server now.

Films between 126 and 129 minutes were unfindable by runtime: “Up to 2 hours” ended at 125 and the next step started at 130. The steps now meet exactly — and “May be long” is honestly called “Over 2 hours”, because that is what it was built as.
Every series query sent an ineffective parameter to TMDB (`watch_region` without `with_watch_providers`). Removed.

0.16.0.lead: Nexview now does children. A parent creates logins for their own children, the children get a completely separate app built for them — and whatever they wish for is decided first by the parent and only then by you.

sections.title: Creating child accounts
sections.body: Name, password, age, language and a few categories — that is all a child account needs. No email address, no Plex account. Who may create them is your call: the “May create child accounts” checkbox sits in user management. Without it the tab still appears, explains the feature and its limits, and offers a button that files the request as a ticket. That ticket then carries a button which grants the permission in one click and closes it.

sections.title: The children's view
sections.where: Signing in with the child's login
sections.body: A child does not get Nexview with fewer buttons, it gets its own app: bright and colourful instead of dark grey and red, three large destinations along the bottom, no bell, no tickets, no settings. The start page shows the enabled categories as picture tiles; behind each one sit all the titles at once, split into “You can watch these now” and “You can wish for these”. Search stays inside the enabled categories.

sections.title: Wishing, not requesting
sections.body: A child does not request anything — it wishes, and nothing happens until the parent decides. Approving turns the wish into an ordinary request in **their** name: their quota, their profile blocks, their usual path — and you approve the download at the end, as always. Declining takes a short note the child gets to read. The child sees its own list with four plain states: waiting, on its way, it is here, not this time.

sections.title: “View as …”
sections.where: Profile → Children, yellow button on a child
sections.body: The button opens the child's app exactly as the child sees it — same view, same rules, only without the wish button. Checking what actually reaches your child should not require borrowing their password.

sections.title: What this **cannot** do
sections.where: Profile → Children, question mark next to “Child accounts”
sections.body: The limit only applies inside Nexview. Whatever gets approved and downloaded ends up in the same library — what a child can reach in Plex is decided there. And the age ratings come from TMDB, not from us: they can be missing or wrong. Both are stated plainly in the help window, so nobody relies on something that was never promised.

sections.title: Release notes for the last five versions
sections.where: About Nexview → Everything that is new
sections.body: This window now keeps the notes for the last five versions, with a switch per version at the top. Skipping a version — updating the container later, two releases in one day — no longer means never learning what was in it. A dot marks what has arrived since your last “got it”, and the About page brings you back here any time.

small: The per-account age restriction is gone from user management: anyone with a full account is treated as an adult. Existing limits are cleared on the first start — child accounts of course keep theirs.
New mail switch “Your children's wishes” — only visible for accounts that actually have an active child account.
Taking the permission away again deactivates that person's child accounts instead of deleting them. You should be able to reverse a decision without losing accounts.
Profile tabs can be addressed directly again (`?reiter=…`), which is how the bell jumps from a child's wish straight to the place it is decided.

0.15.0.lead: This update is almost entirely about one question: who actually occupies how much space? Nexview can now measure quotas in gigabytes instead of counts — with everything that goes with it.

sections.title: Storage quotas
sections.body: Quotas now work either by count (as before) or by occupied storage. Exactly one of the two currencies applies at a time — the choice sits at the top, with the default limit for all accounts below it. Measuring runs in both modes, so you can watch first and limit later. Every switch rebooks all titles to the house inventory and starts every account at zero; a dialog states the real numbers first. The feature deliberately carries an “In Dev” badge.

sections.title: My storage — for every person
sections.body: Everyone sees their occupied space against their limit, and below it every title, largest first. An eye on each row says whether they have watched it: green means watched, and for seasons explicitly “every episode”. Anyone tidying up can filter to “Watched only”.

sections.title: Hand back instead of delete
sections.where: Profile → Storage quota; you decide in the settings
sections.body: “I don't need this” puts a title up for a decision without anything happening yet — it keeps counting until you have decided. For seasons the person states their wish right away: have it deleted, or keep it and only stop the downloading. Your queue then offers three outcomes: to the house (file stays, account freed), delete (with the actual file list in view) or stop following.

sections.title: The recycle bin and the one condition
sections.body: Because Nexview can delete, a recycle bin belongs to it — you can enter it right here, and Radarr and Sonarr do the work. And the condition without which the system does not add up: titles must stay in Radarr and Sonarr. Removing them there while keeping the file creates something Nexview can measure but never delete again.

sections.title: Requesting single seasons
sections.body: Instead of only “whole series”, individual seasons can be picked — with checkboxes, several at once, plus a separate option for future seasons. Whatever is already there or requested is greyed out rather than hidden. Fixed along the way: Sonarr sometimes unmonitored freshly added shows again; Nexview now notices and repairs that by itself.

sections.title: Deleting an account — with a decision about the estate
sections.body: Users and approvers request deletion in their profile under “Security”; the request reaches you as a ticket. When deleting you decide per title, by checkbox, whether it moves to the house or gets deleted, and what happens to downloads in progress. Nothing keeps downloading ownerless afterwards.

small: A season counts as downloaded only once every episode is really there — before, Nexview reported several seasons finished at once.
Notifications about seasons name the season — in the bell, in the channels and by mail.
4K and 1080p are kept apart properly: a running request in one tier no longer blocks the other.
A 4K file in the regular Radarr is no longer mistaken for a separate 4K copy.
A title that vanished from Radarr or Sonarr no longer stays on “searching” forever.
Free disk space no longer counts the same volume twice.

backups.title: Backups
backups.intro: Nexview writes a copy of its own before every schema change. **But that copy sits in the same directory as the database** — lose the volume and it goes with it. It only becomes a backup once you download it and keep it somewhere else.
backups.createSub: Takes a few seconds and does not disturb anything that is running.
backups.noteHint: What is this backup for? “Before the big cleanup” will help you more in three months than a date.
backups.downloadWhat: You get an **encrypted ZIP** holding the database and the key file `secret.key`. The key has to come along, otherwise the stored credentials for Radarr, Sonarr, TMDB and the mail server cannot be read later. Caches are left out — Nexview fetches those again on its own.
backups.passwordWarning: **Remember this password.** There is no second key and no way back: without it the file is worthless. The archive opens with 7-Zip, WinRAR or your file manager — so you do not depend on Nexview to get at your own data.
backups.loadFailed: The list could not be loaded.
backups.folderHint: The files live in `{{ordner}}`. They are **not** reachable through the web server — only through this button and through the file system.
backups.keepHint: Only **automatic** copies are capped — ones you made by hand stay, however many there are. Now that caches are left out, a copy costs a few MB; twenty of them reach back months.
backups.deleteWarning: Gone is gone. If you might still need this one, download it first.

restore.passwordHint: The password you set when you downloaded it.
restore.tooNew: This backup comes from version **{{version}}** and is therefore **newer** than the one running. Nexview can only carry data forward, never back — restoring it would damage the installation. Update Nexview first.
restore.unknownVersion: This backup does not say which version it came from. Without that there is no way to tell whether it fits.
restore.envKeyWarning: **Careful: `NEXVIEW_SECRET_KEY` is set as an environment variable.** The variable always wins, so the key inside the archive is ignored. If its value differs from the one the backup was made with, **none of the stored credentials can be read afterwards** — Radarr, Sonarr, TMDB, the mail server and every media server would have to be connected again.
restore.freshNote: Nexview writes a backup of the current (empty) state first — if something is wrong with the archive, that is the way back.
restore.replaceWarning: **This replaces the entire database.** Everything that happened since this backup is gone afterwards: accounts, requests, ratings, watchlists. Everyone signed in is signed out, including you. Nexview writes a backup of the current state first — that is the way back.
restore.title: Restore a backup
restore.adminIntro: Replaces the running installation with the state from a backup. **Everything that happened since is lost.** Nexview writes a backup of the current state first.
restore.outsideWarning: **Only Nexview is rolled back.** Whatever happened in Radarr, Sonarr or on the media server in the meantime stays as it is — deleted movies do not come back. The next sync brings Nexview in line with reality and may cancel requests again, notifications included.

apikeys.title: API tokens
apikeys.intro: For scripts, dashboards and anything that talks to Nexview without a browser. **A token has exactly your permissions** — no more. Send it as `Authorization: Bearer …`.
apikeys.nameHint: For example “home dashboard” or “backup script”. Helps you later when revoking.
apikeys.readOnlyHint: Can fetch data but not create, change or delete anything. Right for dashboards and monitoring.
apikeys.onlyOnce: **Copy it now.** This token is never shown again — not even an administrator can look it up. If you lose it, create a new one.
apikeys.howToUse: Usage: send the header `Authorization: Bearer <token>` with every request.
apikeys.revokeWarning: It stops working immediately. Anything using it is locked out.
